opening_summary: Thirty-two terms for planning, routing, recording and finishing a film that moves a camera through a game you built, and for proving that what the film says is true.
opening_description: 32 terms to plan, shoot and check a game film.

idea.narration: Hallo. This is Liam, in for Bear. Newcomers often think a walkthrough film is there to make a game look good. It is not. It shows what the game really does, from real captures, and says plainly what it leaves out. This film goes through the terms for planning, routing, recording and checking such a film, each one shown.
idea.text:
A walkthrough film
makes the game look good.
idea.replacementWords: shows what the game really does

beats.narration: This table is the map, thirty-two terms in four groups for a film that moves a camera through a game. The first group, Plan it, holds walkthrough film, central idea, beat, beat sheet, storyboard, script, voice-over and pacing, what the film says, in what order, for how long.

The second group, Route it, holds shot, route, waypoint, establishing shot, camera move and route check. These terms say where the camera goes, and how you check that its path is allowed before a single frame is made.

The third group, Record it, holds real-time capture, render, fixed frame rate, deterministic capture, frame rate, frame count, resolution and aspect ratio. These terms say how the frames of the film are made.

The fourth group, Finish and check, holds cut and transition, b-roll, title card, safe margins, captions, decibel, loudness, what it is not, call to action, and claim versus evidence. These terms say how the film is put together, and how it is proved honest.

A drawing of a level, with a red camera frame sweeping across it. A Walkthrough film is a narrated camera tour of a game or an asset. It shows what the thing really does, from real captures, and says what it leaves out. Its parts are camera moves, voice-over, and a plain statement of what it is not. For example, a student films one level of their platformer up to the flag, while the narration says there is no save system yet.

Central idea is the one sentence every shot in the film must serve. A shot that does not serve it is cut, even a good-looking one. In this made-up example the idea is that level one teaches the jump. Four of six candidate shots serve it, and the menu music reel and the credits scroll are cut. For example, if a student's film is about how an enemy patrols, a pretty shot of the title menu does not belong in it.

A Beat is one unit of the film, one picture, one idea, and the words spoken over it. In this made-up beat the picture is the jump over the first gap, the idea is that a longer press jumps farther, and its thirteen words take five point four seconds at two point four words a second. For example, one beat might show the player touching a coin while a single line says that each coin adds to the score.

A Beat sheet is the whole film as a table, each beat's picture, words and length, in order. It is also the shot list, one row per shot. Here six made-up beats run six plus twelve plus eighteen plus twenty plus sixteen plus ten, eighty-two seconds, a sum and not a target. A storyboard has only pictures, and a beat sheet adds words and seconds. For example, a student lists each beat of their platformer film, with its line and its seconds, before capturing anything.

Four rough frames, a gap, a jump, a spike and a flag. A Storyboard is a set of rough drawings of the key frames, in order, made before anything is captured. It fixes what each picture will show, with no words and no seconds yet. For example, before recording a film of their dungeon game, a student sketches four boxes on paper, the door, the first enemy, the key and the exit, one per beat.

Under each frame now sits a line of narration. The Script is those words, written out and checked before anyone records them. Written under each frame, they can be counted and cut. Here the four lines have nine, fourteen, fifteen and seventeen words. The script is the words on paper, and the voice-over is the same words spoken. For example, a student filming a racing game writes the line for the first corner, counts its words, and trims it before recording.

Voice-over is narration heard over the pictures, while the speaker is never shown in the shot. Speaking takes time. At two point four words a second, nine words take three point eight seconds, and seventeen take seven point one. The four lines add up to twenty-two point nine seconds of speech. For example, in a film of a puzzle game, the narrator explains how a switch opens a door while the viewer sees only the game, never the narrator.

Pacing is how long each beat lasts, set by the stretch of route the camera must cover and the time its words need. Speech must fit its beat. Beats one and three fit. Beat two has five point eight seconds of speech in a five second beat, so two words go, and beat four loses one word. You cut words, not footage. For example, the line spoken while the camera crosses a bridge in a student's level must end before the camera leaves the bridge.

A top view of a level, thirty-eight by twenty-two metres, with walls and five small landmarks. A Shot is one continuous camera take, with a job, revealing something no earlier shot did. This one covers the first leg, nine metres at one metre a second, so nine seconds. The route is the whole path, and a shot is one take along part of it. For example, one shot follows a student's player character from the start to the first pit, without a cut.

Route is the planned path the camera travels through the scene, measured before any frame is rendered. Here the camera runs the whole red line, forty-three metres. Divide that length by the speed, one metre a second, and you get the running time, forty-three seconds. For example, before recording a film of a cave level, a student plans the camera's path from the entrance, past the bats, to the treasure room, and measures how long it is.

A Waypoint is a point along the route where the camera passes, turns or stops. Five numbered waypoints split this route into four legs, nine, ten, fourteen and ten metres, forty-three in all. Each leg can be its own shot, and the waypoints turn a wish for the camera into numbers. For example, a student puts one waypoint at the level's start, one where the camera turns toward a moving platform, and one at the goal flag, where it stops.

An Establishing shot is a wide opening shot that shows where everything is before any nearer view. The red frame takes in all five landmarks at once. The black box, the first nearer view, holds only one of the five. For example, a walkthrough of a small arena game might open on the whole arena from above, so the viewer knows where the spawn points and the exit are before the camera moves in on the player.

Four small top views, a pan, a dolly in, a truck and an orbit. A Camera move is what the camera itself does, such as turning on the spot, moving toward the subject, sliding sideways, or circling it. Each one can be measured. This pan turns forty degrees in four seconds, ten degrees a second, under a limit of thirty. For example, in a film of their level, a slow orbit around a statue the student modelled in Blender shows it from every side.

A Route check is a script that steps through every frame of the route, measuring speed, turn rate, roll and height. The camera move is what the camera does, and the route check says whether it is allowed. Over thirty metres in twenty-four seconds, linear keys hold one point two five metres a second, while an ease from rest peaks at one point nine six, over the one point five limit. For example, a student checks the path through their forest level before recording.

The route check's result as a table, with made-up measured values. Linear speed, turn rate, roll and eye height pass. Eased speed, one point nine six metres a second, fails. One fail sends you back to fix the route, not the report, and the limits are starting points, not standards. For example, if the camera dips below eye height on a staircase in a student's level, they raise the path and run the route check again.

Milliseconds per frame for thirty-six frames of a simulated run. Real-time capture means recording the game while it runs, at whatever pace the machine manages, so frame times vary. The dashed line is the sixty frames per second budget, sixteen point seven milliseconds. Nine of thirty-six frames took over one and a half times that, so the take is hard to repeat. For example, a student screen-records their platformer while playing it, and a busy explosion makes some frames late.
figures: 9 of 36 frames took over 1.5 times the budget

beats.narration: Render means computing each frame offline, as slowly as needed, then joining the frames into a film. In this simulated case a ten second film at thirty frames per second is three hundred frames, and at four seconds a frame it takes twenty minutes. Slow is fine, but a render proves nothing about how fast the game runs. For example, a student lets Blender render a turntable of their model overnight, frame by frame, for a smooth clip of it.

Fixed frame rate means every frame stands for exactly the same slice of game time, one divided by the frame rate, whatever the machine does. At a fixed thirty frames per second each frame is thirty-three point three milliseconds of game time, so thirty-six frames are one point two seconds on any machine. For example, a student launches their game from the command line with Godot's fixed frame rate option, so even a slow laptop moves the game forward by the same step each frame.

Deterministic capture gives the same frames every take, from a fixed frame rate, the same inputs and the same route. In this simulation, game time reaches one second on frame thirty-eight in one real-time take and frame forty-eight in another. At a fixed sixty frames per second it lands on frame sixty, take after take. For example, a student records a jump with scripted inputs at a fixed rate, labels it as scripted, and a second take matches the first, frame for frame.

Rows of tick marks, one second each. Frame rate is how many frames are shown each second. The top row has twenty-four ticks, the middle thirty, and the red row sixty. Film often uses twenty-four or thirty, and games sixty. Resolution counts pixels in one frame, and frame rate counts frames in one second. For example, a student sets their walkthrough capture to sixty frames per second so their character's fast dash stays smooth.

Frame count is frame rate times duration, the number of frames the film needs. For a ten second film that is two hundred forty frames at twenty-four, three hundred at thirty, and six hundred at sixty. Every frame is stored or rendered, so sixty frames per second doubles the work of thirty. For example, before rendering a boss fight clip from their game, a student works out its frame count to see how many frames the render must make.

Resolution is the width and height of a frame in pixels. The nested boxes share one shape and hold about zero point nine two, two point zero seven, and eight point two nine million pixels. Doubling width and height gives four times the pixels. Native capture means three thousand eight hundred forty by two thousand one hundred sixty from the start, not scaled up. For example, a student captures their game at that size so the small numbers on the score display stay sharp.

Aspect ratio is width divided by height. A landscape sixteen by nine frame is one point seven eight, a tall nine by sixteen frame is zero point five six, and a square is exactly one. Turned on its side, a frame keeps its pixels but not its aspect. A landscape film and a vertical clip are two renders, not one crop. For example, for a phone-shaped clip, a student renders again in the tall shape instead of cutting the sides off the wide film.

Two five second clips, joined two ways. A Cut jumps straight to the next shot. A Transition, such as a dissolve, overlaps the two shots for a moment. With a hard cut each clip stays whole, ten seconds in all. A one second dissolve eats its overlap, so the pair lasts nine seconds. For example, a student cuts straight from the player at the castle door to the player inside, but dissolves slowly from the day version of a level to the night version.

B-roll is extra footage laid over the main capture. The main capture carries the claim, and the b-roll only decorates it. Here three seconds of b-roll sit over ten seconds of real capture, the narration runs unbroken, and the film is still ten seconds long. Constructed b-roll is labelled as constructed. For example, while the capture shows the player crossing a bridge, a student cuts in a short shot of the bridge model turning on its own, labelled as a constructed view.

A Title card is a full-screen card carrying the film's name, shown briefly at the start and at the end. Here it reads Walker Jumpman, a walkthrough. In this made-up film it takes six seconds of eighty-two, about seven percent, the shortest beat of the film. For example, a student opens the film of their dungeon game with a dark card naming the game, and shows the same card again for a moment at the very end.

A frame three thousand eight hundred forty by two thousand one hundred sixty, with a dashed box inside. Safe margins are that inner area, inset about five percent on each side, where text and logos must sit. That is one hundred ninety-two pixels at each side and one hundred eight at top and bottom. The red bar is text in the margin, which some screens crop. For example, a student places each level's name label inside the dashed line, never along the top edge.

Captions are the narration as text, burned into the picture or kept in a separate subtitle file, each line with a start and an end time. This line, Walker stands at the first gap, runs from second one to second four. Thirty-one characters in three seconds is about ten characters a second. Captions are text you see, and the voice-over is sound you hear. For example, a student's film of their stealth game shows a caption under each spoken line, inside the safe area.
figures: 31 characters in 3.0 s = 10.3 characters a second

beats.narration: Bars of amplitude beside their values in decibels. Decibel, written dB, or dBFS, is a logarithmic unit of loudness. Halving the amplitude is about minus six decibels, and a tenth is minus twenty. In digital audio, zero dBFS, decibels relative to full scale, is the largest level, and everything sits below it. For example, when a student turns a coin sound in their game down to minus six decibels, its wave becomes about half as tall.

Loudness, in LUFS, loudness units relative to full scale, is how loud the whole film is on average, checked against a target window. One course film measured minus twenty-four point five five, inside a window of minus twenty-eight to minus eighteen. Its true peak, minus two point nine six, sits under a ceiling of minus one, about two decibels to spare. For example, a student measures their finished walkthrough, finds its average below the window, and raises the whole mix.

A row of beat blocks, the second one red. What it is not is a statement, spoken and shown on screen, of what the film leaves out, placed in its first two beats. In this made-up example that is by eighteen seconds of eighty-two, twenty-two percent. One level of real play, but not a finished game, no save or sound yet, not tested by players. For example, a student's film of their tower defence game says early on that only one map exists.
figures: 18 s of 82 s = 22% of the run

beats.narration: A Call to action is the last request to the viewer, one concrete thing to try, with a way to check it worked. Here, widen the first gap from three metres to four, run the jump test, and watch whether Walker still clears it. The check is that the test exits with zero, not a vague try it yourself. For example, a student ends by asking viewers to raise the enemy's speed value and see whether the patrol test still passes.

Claim versus evidence separates what the film asserts from the capture or output on screen that backs it. Of five claims, three are backed by clips, the gap, the spike reset and the flag. The claim, it runs at sixty frames per second, has no measurement on screen, and the claim, players love it, has no playtest, so those two are cut or proved. For example, a student who says their enemy chases the player around a wall shows the captured run of it.

Each pair sets two look-alike terms side by side. Real-time capture records the game as it runs, so frame times wobble, like the uneven dark bars. Render computes each frame offline, so every red bar is built to order and even.

Resolution counts the pixels in one frame, here forty cells in one picture. Frame rate counts the frames in one second, here twenty-four pictures. A sharper picture and a smoother motion are different numbers.
A Cut jumps straight to the next shot, so two five second clips make ten seconds. A Transition overlaps the two shots, so a one second dissolve leaves nine.
A Storyboard is pictures in order, with no words and no seconds. A Beat sheet is pictures, words and seconds, here six, twelve and eighteen seconds for the first three beats.

A vague request sits above the exact instruction that replaces it. Make the camera smoother becomes, linear keys at one point two five metres a second, and ease only at rest. A sine ease would peak at one point nine six, over the limit of one point five.

Make it sharper becomes, capture natively at three thousand eight hundred forty by two thousand one hundred sixty, four times the pixels of ten eighty p, not seven twenty p scaled up. That is eight point two nine million pixels against two point zero seven million.
The voice runs past the shot becomes, cut seventeen words to sixteen, so the speech, now six point seven seconds, fits the seven second beat. Speech must end by the time the beat does.
Keep text away from the edge becomes, keep text inside the five percent safe area, one hundred ninety-two pixels at the sides, and one hundred eight at top and bottom.

Make the sound right becomes, integrated loudness between minus twenty-eight and minus eighteen LUFS, and a true peak below minus one. One course film measured minus twenty-four point five five, with a true peak of minus two point nine six. One window, one ceiling.
This is a checklist of six questions to ask before you show a walkthrough film. First, does every shot serve the one-sentence central idea? A shot that does not is cut.
Second, does the film say what it is not in its first two beats, spoken aloud and shown on screen as well?
Third, was the route measured before anything was captured? The route check reports speed, turn rate and height on every frame, against its limits.
Fourth, is every clip real capture of the game? Anything else, such as a mock-up or a staged view, is labelled constructed on screen.
Fifth, do the words fit each beat, and does the sound fit its loudness window? Cut words to fit the beat, and measure the film against the window.
Sixth, does every claim in the narration have evidence on screen? Then say it exactly. Not make it smoother, but one point two five metres a second, linear, under one point five.

recap_lines: A beat sheet lists every beat's picture, words and seconds, in order.
A shot is one take, and the route is the whole path.
A route check measures speed, turn rate, roll and height on every frame.
A fixed frame rate gives every frame the same slice of game time.
Resolution is pixels in one frame, and frame rate is frames per second.
Every claim in the narration needs evidence on screen.

your_turn.segment: Name The Film Term, Defend It
your_turn.command: Quiz me on walkthrough film terms with short cases from filming a game I built, one at a time. Use beat sheet, storyboard, shot, route, waypoint, real-time capture, render, fixed frame rate, resolution and b-roll. For each case I must name the exact term and say why its look-alike is wrong. Hold back the answer until I reply, then tell me if I was right.
checks: Check: each case is about filming a game, and the answer waits for you.
Check: you named the exact term and said why its look-alike is wrong.

deck_problems: Source lines on slides 6, 7, 8, 9, 11 and 12 misspell the skill as 'godot-waikthrough SKILL.md'; Assignment 10 calls it godot-walkthrough.
Slide 11 step 1: the tall bars of the real-time capture animation are drawn over the heading, so it shows as 'Real-ti  cap re'.

Slide 10 step 1: the definition places the disclosure 'in the first two shots', while the summary line and the slide 13 checklist say 'first two beats'; the summary line also says 'Say what the model is not' where the film or game is meant.

Slide 5: Camera move is defined only as 'Pan, tilt, dolly, truck, orbit and the rest, defined in the 18 Camera deck', with the heading '(REF: TERMS - CAMERA)'. The term has no meaning of its own on the slide, and the pointer to another deck by number cannot be spoken in a self-contained film. The narration defines the four moves from the course glossary.

Badges: slide 3 and slide 8 carry 'Computed', but their beat lengths and the 82 s film are the invented example from slide 2 ('Illustrative data'); only the arithmetic is computed. Slide 3's notes say so; slide 8's do not.
Slide 7 step 2: under 'FRAMES IN A 10 S FILM' the tick rows still show one second of ticks (24, 30, 60), not 240, 300 and 600 frames; the summary line also breaks '10 / s' across two lines.
Slide 11 step 4: the beat sheet side says 'words and seconds per beat' but the picture shows only seconds bars, no words.
Slide 6 step 1: 'mean 24.8 ms = 40.4 fps'. 1000 / 24.8 = 40.3; 40.4 holds only if the unrounded mean is 24.76 ms or less. Worth checking the rounding.
Slide 12 step 1: 'Linear keys at 1.25 m/s; ease only at rest' is unclear (ease only where the camera starts or stops from rest?). The narration keeps the slide's wording.
Slide 3 step 2: the example script says Walker 'restarts at the last checkpoint'; the reference files do not mention checkpoints in Walker. The narration does not repeat it.
Slide 0 notes say 'Deck 10 of the topic order' while the file is deck 21; fine if topic order differs from file order.
